md_sign_wall.blurb: Sign Wall is one of the busier faces on the Maryland Heights cliff above Harpers Ferry, easy to spot by the big faded painted advertisement high on the rock. It is mainly a trad wall: nearly all of its 14 lines are gear-protected, many of them multi-pitch, with a single top-rope option. Grades run from low fifth class up to the 5.12 range, but the bulk sit between 5.8 and 5.10, so it suits climbers comfortable leading moderate trad. Most of the stone is solid, though the section above and to the right of the sign is loose and sharp. The way down is by rappel.

md_main_wall_the.blurb: The Main Wall is the leftmost section of Wolf Rock in Catoctin Mountain Park, right beside the trail near Thurmont. It holds 14 short, easy climbs on blocky, cracked quartzite: mostly trad lines plus a pair of top-ropes, running from the very easiest grades up to about 5.6. Many lines are only a few body-lengths tall and not far from a scramble, with slabby ground and plenty of cracks, so it works well for beginners learning to place gear or build anchors. A steep, rocky hike of roughly a mile gets you there, so expect a warm-up before you rack up.

md_1_the_bouldering_pit.blurb: The Bouldering Pit is a small boulder cluster in the Thurmont Watershed, part of the TWS Rocks zone near Thurmont. Two rocks meet to form a pocket with a cleared, level floor, which gives good landings. It holds 14 problems, nearly all of them easy to moderate: one beginner-level problem, a handful of V0 to V1, a few V2s, and one V3 and one V4 for the stronger boulderer. Reaching it means taking the east-side trail, then following the old road bed through a boulder field, so footing is loose and leafy. Bring pads and plan on a short session.

md_south_end_the.blurb: The South End is the southernmost outcrop on the cliff band at Annapolis Rock, a quartzite crag on South Mountain west of Frederick. Of its 15 climbs, almost all are trad, with one top-rope line, and the range is wide, from easy fifth class through the 5.12 range, with most lines between 5.8 and 5.11. The cliffs here have no bolts, so leaders need a trad rack, and top-ropers need webbing or a long static line for natural anchors; anchors are easier to build here than on some neighbouring walls. Reach it by following the trail or scrambling along the cliff base.
md_south_end_the.parking_note: Leave the car at the roadside Appalachian Trail lot on Route 40 near Myersville, then hike the trail to the overlook before dropping to the cliffs.

md_earth_buttress.blurb: Earth Buttress is a top-rope-only buttress on the Cumberland Narrows cliffs above Cumberland, the third buttress north of Moonshine Buttress along the clifftop trail. All 14 lines are top-rope problems: one very easy route, about nine at 5.7, a few at 5.8 and one 5.9, so it is a friendly place for moderate climbers. The routes face southwest and catch sun from roughly midday into the evening. Getting to the base means rappelling in or down-climbing a chimney, so bring a rope and anchor material for the top.
